note: Practical units for the Israel track, in the style of a structured conversation course: each unit groups existing lessons by the situation they prepare for (core = beginner il lessons, more = the B1 lessons that open after the capstone), with short grammar notes, a spaced unit review, and listening and speaking drills built from the lessons' own words, clips and exercises. Every Hebrew example is a verbatim string from that unit's own lessons (tests/curriculum.israel-units.test.js checks it); no Hebrew was written for this file. Grammar notes are original English and have not been reviewed by a native speaker or teacher.

units.title: Hello and Introductions
units.can: Greet, thank, say sorry, and say who you are and where you are from

grammar.point: No word for 'am' or 'is' in the present: Hebrew just puts the two parts side by side.
'You' changes for a man and a woman, and so does the question that uses it.

examples.en: what is your name (to a man)
what is your name (to a woman)

units.title: Sound Like a Local
units.can: Use the small words Israelis fill a conversation with, and put the stress where they do

grammar.point: Most Hebrew words are stressed on the last syllable; English speakers tend to stress too early.

examples.en: how are you (to a man): shlom-KHA

grammar.point: Fillers carry the tone of a whole sentence; 'nu' can mean 'well?', 'so?' or 'come on'.

units.title: Numbers and Prices
units.can: Count, understand a price in shekels and ask how much

grammar.point: When you simply count (one, two, three) Israelis use the feminine forms.
'Kama' asks both 'how much' and 'how many'.

units.title: Cafe and Ordering Food
units.can: Order a coffee the way you like it, eat in or take away, and ask for the bill

grammar.point: 'Efshar' plus a verb in the 'to ...' form is the polite way to ask for something.
'Bli' means 'without' and goes straight before the noun.
The verb follows the speaker: a man says rotzeh, a woman says rotzah.

examples.en: I would like a coffee (said by a man)
I would like a coffee (said by a woman)

units.title: Shopping and Paying
units.can: Ask if something is there, ask the price, bargain a little and pay

grammar.point: 'Yesh' (there is) and 'ein' (there isn't) never change, whatever follows them.
'How much does it cost' is literally 'how much does this go up'.

units.title: Getting Around
units.can: Take a bus, train or taxi, ask the way and follow directions

grammar.point: An ending -ah on a place word can mean 'towards': right becomes 'to the right'.
Commands change for a woman.

units.title: Time, Plans and the Phone
units.can: Say when, make a plan, and arrange or move a meeting by phone or message

grammar.point: The future for 'I' starts with e- (or a- before some letters).
Days of the week are mostly numbered: Sunday is 'the first day'; Saturday is Shabbat.

units.title: Verbs: Now and Yesterday
units.can: Say what you do now and what you did yesterday

grammar.point: Present tense works like an adjective: it changes for man, woman and plural, not for I, you or he.
Past tense marks the person on the end of the verb: -ti is 'I'.

units.title: People, Family and Opinions
units.can: Talk about your family, ask about someone's children and say what you think

grammar.point: 'I have' is 'yesh li': there is to me.
Age is asked as 'son of how much' or 'daughter of how much'.

examples.en: how old are you? (to a man)
how old are you? (to a woman)

units.title: Health, Help and Emergencies
units.can: Say what hurts, get medicine, see a doctor and call for help

grammar.point: Symptoms use 'yesh li', I have.
'It hurts me' puts the person after the verb.

units.title: Home, Work and Study
units.can: Book a room, rent and fix an apartment, handle the bank and post office, and talk about work and study

grammar.point: 'Ani mechapes' (I'm looking for) takes the thing straight after it, with no 'for'.
'Rotzeh' (want) plus a 'to ...' verb says what you want to do.

examples.en: I want to withdraw money (said by a man)

units.title: Israeli Life: Weather, Outings and Holidays
units.can: Talk about the weather, go out, accept a Shabbat invitation and give the right holiday greeting

grammar.point: How you feel uses 'to me': 'kar li' is 'I'm cold'; without 'li' it describes the day.
Greetings belong to a time: Shabbat shalom until Shabbat ends, then shavua tov.

units.title: Capstone Conversation
units.can: Hold a five-minute conversation: greet, buy something, ask the way and make a plan

grammar.point: Everything so far in one talk; when you are stuck, ask for it again instead of switching to English.

examples.en: explain it to me (to a man)
